title: Box Packer
context: Grade 5, the last worked examples on volume and Exercise 8.4. An adult sees a formula and a division. What the pages are doing is reading length x breadth as one base area, working back to a height, and counting how many small cubes fit a box, where the division of volumes is right only when each edge takes a whole number of cubes.

writeup.why: Find a volume as base area x height, work back to a height from a volume and a base area, find a block's volume from equal cubes, and check how many small cubes really fit along each edge of a box.
writeup.look: A base tile that rises into a solid, a volume card and Height dial on the second phase, a row of equal cubes on the third, and an open box with small cubes and the Divide card on the last.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Box Packer' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number of small cubes packed or joined. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The base tile lies at x 160, y 520, 400 by 120, deep blue, labelled Given with its area. The Height handle is a round grip at its right edge; each unit of height it raises adds one base's worth to the running volume, written beside the solid at x 600, y 300. The volume card and the Height dial stand at x 820, y 250 and x 820, y 340, and the Check line runs along y 690 from x 120. On the third phase the row of equal cubes lies along y 500 from x 160, and the Join button stands at x 820, y 420. On the fourth phase the open box stands in three visible faces at x 160, y 260 inside a box 600 by 400 with its edges labelled; the Pack edge button at x 820, y 420 lays whole cubes along one edge at a time, and any space too small for a whole cube turns rose, labelled Left over. The Divide card stands at x 820, y 520. The answer reached is green. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with cm, sq. cm and cu. cm keys. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the ten tools of this chapter share them. The lengths the question gives, as a side, a length, a breadth, a height, an edge or a base area, are deep blue, labelled Given or by their own name. The perimeter, area, volume or missing side the working reaches is green, labelled Answer. The boundary that a perimeter walks round is vermilion, labelled Boundary. The unit being counted, one unit square, one unit cube, one row or one layer, is violet, labelled Unit square, Unit cube, Row or Layer. The part squares of an estimate and the space left over where no whole cube fits are rose, labelled More than half, Half or Left over. The side, square, cube, layer or step being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open, and nothing on this stage is ever grey. A square or cube that is not being counted stays warm white inside its near-black outline, grid lines, unit words and signs are near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength. Chrome never borrows one of them, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The last box stays packed with its whole cubes and its rose Left over strip, and the answer in green beside the Divide card.

source_tool.description: A base tile lies flat on a table top, deep blue, labelled Given with its area. The child drags a Height handle upward, and the tile rises into a solid, one layer of the base's area for each unit of height, with the running volume beside it. On the second phase a volume card is given and a Height dial raises the base try by try until base area x height meets the card, with a Check line that multiplies back. On the third phase a row of equal small cubes, each labelled with its edge, slides together into a block at a tap of Join, and the working line writes the count times one cube's volume. On the last phase an open box is drawn in three faces with its edges labelled, and a Pack edge button lays small cubes along one edge at a time; whole cubes only go in, and any space too small for a whole cube turns rose, labelled Left over. A Divide card beside the box shows the box's volume divided by one cube's volume, set against the cubes packed. A number pad types a volume, a height or a count. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of small cubes packed or joined.
source_tool.art_direction: Packing cubes into a cardboard box / Picture book

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: squared paper with equal square cells, rulers marked in centimetres, unit cubes that stack into rows, layers and cuboids, open boxes, and clear jars of water with a level line.
Every figure is drawn to one scale inside its stage, so a side twice as long looks twice as long, and every square cell and every unit cube in one picture is the same size.
Every side, edge and measure carries its unit: cm or m for a length, sq. cm or sq. m for an area, and cu. cm or cu. m for a volume. The longer side of a rectangle is always the one labelled length.
A cuboid is drawn in three visible faces, and a cube only when all its edges are equal. Cubes hidden behind or under others are shown by a see-through layer when they are counted.
A part square on an estimate is marked by its kind, more than half, half or less than half, in words; no cross ever marks a square that is counted.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: a walker tracing a boundary, rows of squares filling a rectangle, layers of cubes stacking into a cuboid, or water rising in a jar.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a square, a cube or a number the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a measure plays in a piece of working: the lengths the question gives, as a side, a length, a breadth, a height, an edge or a base area, are deep blue, and the perimeter, area, volume or missing side the working reaches is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The boundary that a perimeter walks round is vermilion. The unit being counted, one unit square, one unit cube, one row or one layer, is violet. The part squares an area estimate rounds, and the space left over where no whole cube fits, are rose. The side, square, cube, layer or step being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open and is not used here. A square or cube that is not being counted stays warm white inside its outline, and grid lines and unit words are near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Boundary, Unit square, Unit cube, Layer, More than half, Half and Left over, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Pack that edge again, one whole cube at a time.
voice.onNext: A new box. Look at the base first.
voice.opening: A base, a box and some cubes.
voice.onFinish: You checked every edge before trusting a division.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Raise a base or pack a box of your own.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has measured a small box and one cube, divided the volumes on paper, and then packed the box with whole cubes by hand. The tool is what packs edge by edge beside the division, so the two can disagree on screen as they did on the desk.

answer_key.rule: The base area of a cuboid is length x breadth, so its volume is base area x height. A height is the number that times the base area gives the volume; check by multiplying back. A block made of equal cubes has a volume of the count times one cube's volume. To find how many small cubes fit in a box, check how many fit along each edge, whole cubes only, and multiply those numbers. A space left over along any edge means fewer cubes fit than a division of the volumes gives.
answer_key.wrong: The cubes the child packed stay in the box, and the stage packs the edge in question again beside it, one whole cube at a time, lighting the space left over rose and the edge amber. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The base area is length x breadth, already multiplied.
So the volume is base area x height.
24 x 7 = 168, so the volume is 168 cu. cm.
items.question: A box has a base of 24 sq. cm and a height of 7 cm. What is its volume?
items.checkpoint: Base area times height gives the volume.
items.misconception: Adding the base area and the height, which mixes a surface with a length.

steps: Base area x height is the volume, so 34 x height gives 204.
Try 5: 34 x 5 = 170, which is too small.
Try 6: 34 x 6 = 204, so the tank is 6 m high.
items.question: A tank has a volume of 204 cu. m and a base of 34 sq. m. How high is it?
items.checkpoint: Multiply back to check the height.
items.misconception: Multiplying the volume by the base area, which gives a far bigger number, not a height.

steps: One small cube has a volume of 5 x 5 x 5 = 125 cu. cm.
The block is made of 6 of them.
6 x 125 = 750, so the block is 750 cu. cm.
items.question: A block is cut into 6 equal cubes of edge 5 cm. What is the volume of the block?
items.misconception: Multiplying the count by the edge instead of by one cube's volume.

steps: The box has a volume of 9 x 6 x 4 = 216 cu. cm.
One 3 cm cube has a volume of 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 cu. cm.
Dividing the volumes, 216 divided by 27 is 8, but check how many fit along each edge.
Along the 9 cm edge 3 fit. Along the 6 cm edge 2 fit.
Along the 4 cm edge only 1 fits, with 1 cm left over.
So only six whole cubes fit, not eight: three along one edge, two along the next and one along the last.
items.question: How many 3 cm cubes really fit in a box 9 cm by 6 cm by 4 cm?
items.checkpoint: Check each edge before trusting a division of volumes.
items.misconception: Trusting the division of the volumes, which counts pieces of cubes that cannot go in as whole cubes.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: A box has a base of 20 sq. m and a height of 3 m. What is its volume?
A block is made of 10 equal cubes, each with a volume of 8 cu. cm. What is its volume?
A box has a volume of 56 cu. cm and a base of 14 sq. cm. How high is it?
items.final_answer: 14 x 4 = 56, so it is 4 cm high

items.question: A tank has a base of 45 sq. m and a height of 3 m. What is its volume?
A box has a volume of 117 cu. cm and a base of 13 sq. cm. How high is it?
items.final_answer: 13 x 9 = 117, so it is 9 cm high

items.question: A block is made of 4 equal cubes of edge 3 cm. What is its volume?
items.final_answer: One cube is 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 cu. cm. The block is 4 x 27 = 108 cu. cm

items.question: How many 2 cm cubes really fit in a box 10 cm by 4 cm by 3 cm?
items.final_answer: Along the 10 cm edge 5 fit. Along the 4 cm edge 2 fit. Along the 3 cm edge only 1 fits, with 1 cm left over. So 5 x 2 x 1 = 10 whole cubes fit, not the 15 that dividing the volumes gives

items.question: Do 3 cm cubes fill a box 15 cm by 9 cm by 6 cm with no space left over?
items.final_answer: Yes. Along the edges 5, 3 and 2 cubes fit, with nothing left over. So 5 x 3 x 2 = 30 cubes fill it

practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

teaching_notes: Measure a small box and one cube, divide the volumes on paper, then pack the box with whole cubes before the tool opens. Base area times height is length times breadth times height, with the first two already multiplied. Work back to a height by asking what times the base area gives the volume, and multiply back. A block of equal cubes is the count times one cube. Before trusting a division, check how many small cubes fit along each edge; a space left over along any edge means fewer fit. The printed bases, heights and tray are the child's to work.
